title: The Frog
source_note: NCERT structural alignment only. All teaching passages, prompts, examples, answers, and rubrics are original Zidd-authored content and do not copy the textbook body.

levels.title: Life beside land and water
levels.focus: understand frog habitats and amphibious life
levels.teaching_goal: Identify details that show how a frog uses both watery and land habitats.

guided_check.teaching_block: A habitat is the place where a living thing finds food, shelter, and suitable conditions.
guided_check.passage: At sunrise, a frog sits on a damp stone at the edge of a pond. When danger comes, it slips into the water.
guided_check.prompt: Which two parts of the habitat does this frog use?
options: a damp stone and pond water
the damp stone without the pond
pond water without a land resting place
a muddy bank and wet leaves
accepted_answers: a damp stone and pond water
the damp stone and the pond
land beside the pond and water

bridge.teaching_block: An amphibian can use water and land during different parts of its life. Explain both parts instead of selecting a label.
bridge.passage: One frog shelters among wet leaves during the afternoon and returns to a shallow pool at night.
bridge.prompt: Explain how the frog uses two parts of its habitat.

concept_slots.description: Identifies the frog's shelter on land.
Identifies the frog's use of the pool or water.
any_of: uses the shallow pool at night
moves from the leaves to the pool

masterclass.teaching_block: To find a paragraph's main idea, combine repeated details and explain what the habitat provides.
masterclass.passage: Pond frogs hide in reeds, rest on muddy banks, and dive below the surface when startled. Each place helps them meet a different need.
masterclass.prompt: State the main idea and name one shelter place and one escape place.

concept_slots.description: States that the pond habitat provides different useful spaces.
any_of: pond habitat provides different useful places
frog uses different places for different needs
habitat offers places for shelter and escape
pond gives frogs places to rest and escape

concept_slots.description: Names reeds or the bank as a shelter or resting place.
any_of: bank gives it a place to rest

concept_slots.description: Names water as the place used to escape danger.
any_of: dives below the surface to escape

independent_check.teaching_block: Read the new observation and explain the evidence without using answer choices.
independent_check.passage: During a light shower, Neel spots a small animal hopping across moss. Minutes later, only its eyes are visible above a rain-filled ditch.
independent_check.prompt: What evidence suggests that the animal can manage both land and water?

concept_slots.description: Names evidence that the animal moved on land.
Names evidence that the animal entered or used water.
any_of: eyes showed above the ditch water

transfer_check.teaching_block: Apply the land-and-water evidence test to an unfamiliar observation. Name one clue from each setting and explain what the pair shows.
transfer_check.passage: At sunrise, a child sees a green animal spring from a vegetable patch. A moment later, it floats beside the steps of a half-filled water tank.
transfer_check.prompt: Which two clues show that the animal can move in both a land setting and a water setting?

concept_slots.description: Uses the vegetable patch or springing action as evidence from land.
Uses floating beside the tank steps as evidence from water.
any_of: used the water in the tank

levels.title: A changing water life
levels.focus: use context words and summarize the frog life cycle
levels.teaching_goal: Use context to understand life-cycle words and retell the change from egg to adult frog.

guided_check.teaching_block: Nearby words can explain an unfamiliar word. Read what the word names or describes.
guided_check.passage: The pond holds spawn, a soft cluster of frog eggs floating near a water plant.
guided_check.prompt: What does the word spawn mean here?
options: a cluster of frog eggs
a group of newly hatched tadpoles
bubbles gathered around a water plant
insect eggs floating near the surface
accepted_answers: a cluster of frog eggs
frog eggs
a soft group of frog eggs

bridge.teaching_block: Life-cycle clues often name a new body part or an old feature that changes. Describe both changes yourself.
bridge.passage: A tadpole begins with a swimming tail. As it grows, back legs appear and the tail becomes shorter.
bridge.prompt: Describe the two body changes in one sentence.

concept_slots.description: States that legs appear or grow.
any_of: back legs appear on the tadpole
its back legs begin to grow

concept_slots.description: States that the tail becomes shorter.
any_of: tadpole loses most of its tail

masterclass.teaching_block: A clear summary selects the major stages, keeps their order, and leaves out tiny observations.
masterclass.passage: Frog eggs hatch into tadpoles. Tadpoles grow legs, lose most of their tails, and develop into young frogs before becoming adults.
masterclass.prompt: Summarize the life cycle from eggs to adults in one sentence.

concept_slots.description: Includes the egg stage.
Includes the tadpole stage.
Includes development into a young or adult frog.

independent_check.teaching_block: Summarize only the important changes in the fresh field note.
independent_check.passage: Week one: round eggs cling to pond grass. Week three: dark swimmers have long tails. Week seven: the swimmers have four legs and tiny tails.
independent_check.prompt: Summarize the development recorded in the three notes in one sentence.

concept_slots.description: Identifies eggs as the starting stage.
Identifies tadpoles or tailed swimmers as the middle stage.
States that legs develop.
any_of: four legs appear as they grow

concept_slots.description: States that the tail becomes shorter or disappears.
any_of: tails get shorter as legs grow

transfer_check.teaching_block: Use the same change-over-time skill with a different pond animal. Keep the stages in time order and leave out minor details.
transfer_check.passage: A dragonfly begins as an egg near water. A young nymph lives below the surface and grows. Later it climbs a reed, sheds its old covering, and flies away as an adult.
transfer_check.prompt: Summarize the dragonfly's development from egg to adult in one ordered sentence.

concept_slots.description: Begins with the egg stage near water.
Places the growing underwater nymph in the middle.
any_of: next it is a water nymph

concept_slots.description: Ends with the adult leaving the old covering and flying.

forbidden_phrases: nymph lives only in the sky

levels.title: Catch food, avoid hunters
levels.focus: infer how a frog feeds and survives predators
levels.teaching_goal: Explain how a quick tongue, camouflage, and stillness help a frog eat or stay safe.

guided_check.teaching_block: An inference joins an action to its likely purpose. Ask what the action helps the animal do.
guided_check.passage: A beetle crawls close. The frog stays still, then flicks out its sticky tongue in a split second.
guided_check.prompt: Why does the frog use a fast, sticky tongue?
options: to catch the beetle before it escapes
to check whether the beetle is safe to eat
to knock the beetle into the pond for later
to guide a jump towards the beetle
accepted_answers: to catch the beetle before it escapes
it helps the frog catch the beetle quickly
because the sticky tongue traps fast prey

bridge.teaching_block: Camouflage works when an animal's colours or patterns make it hard to notice against its surroundings. Explain the match and its result.
bridge.passage: A mottled brown frog rests without moving among fallen leaves. A snake passes close by but does not turn towards it.
bridge.prompt: Explain how the frog's appearance reduced the danger.

concept_slots.description: States that the frog matched or blended with the leaves.
any_of: brown frog matched the fallen leaves
camouflage blended it with the leaves

concept_slots.description: States that the snake did not notice or see the frog.
any_of: snake did not see the frog
frog stayed hidden from the snake

masterclass.teaching_block: Animals can combine defences. Compare what each strategy does, then explain how the two strategies reduce danger in different ways.
masterclass.passage: A brown frog stays motionless among dead leaves, so its outline is hard to notice. When the leaves shift and expose it, the frog dives beneath the pond surface.
masterclass.prompt: Compare the frog's two defence strategies and explain how each one helps.

concept_slots.description: Explains that stillness and matching leaves make the frog difficult to notice.
any_of: stays still so it is hard to notice
motionless among the leaves hides it
camouflage makes it hard to see

concept_slots.description: Explains that diving underwater moves the frog away when camouflage no longer works.
any_of: dives beneath the surface to get away
moves into the pond when exposed

forbidden_phrases: diving makes it easier to catch
both strategies do the same thing

independent_check.teaching_block: Transfer the two-strategy idea to a new scene. Infer the danger from the clues rather than waiting for it to be named.
independent_check.passage: A wide shadow sweeps over a rocky pool. A speckled frog presses flat against the stones, then slips under a root as the shadow circles back.
independent_check.prompt: How do the frog's two actions reduce the danger in different ways?

concept_slots.description: Explains that pressing against matching stones makes the frog harder to detect.
any_of: presses against the stones to blend in
flat against the stones is hard to see

concept_slots.description: Explains that slipping under the root adds cover or removes the frog from view.
any_of: slips under the root to hide
moves under the root out of sight

transfer_check.teaching_block: Infer how two defensive actions solve different parts of a threat in a new animal scene.
transfer_check.passage: A brown lizard freezes against tree bark when a kite passes overhead. When the bird turns back, the lizard darts into a narrow crack.
transfer_check.prompt: Explain how freezing against the bark and entering the crack protect the lizard in different ways.

concept_slots.description: Explains that stillness and matching bark make the lizard difficult to notice.
any_of: freezes to blend with the bark
staying still makes it hard to notice

concept_slots.description: Explains that the crack provides physical cover from the returning bird.
any_of: darts into the crack to hide
moves inside the crack out of reach
uses the narrow crack as cover

forbidden_phrases: wants the kite to see it

levels.title: Compare swimmers and hoppers
levels.focus: compare frog movement and body features with fish or toads
levels.teaching_goal: Use accurate details to compare how frogs, fish, and toads move and where they live.

guided_check.teaching_block: Strong hind legs push a frog forwards on land, while webbing makes a broader foot that pushes more water during a swim.
guided_check.passage: The frog springs from the bank with its long back legs and then paddles across the pool with its wide back feet.
guided_check.prompt: Which body parts support the two kinds of movement?
options: long back legs and wide back feet
long back legs and narrow front feet
strong front legs and wide back feet
long back legs alone for both movements
accepted_answers: long back legs and wide back feet
its long hind legs and broad webbed feet
back legs for jumping and wide feet for swimming

bridge.teaching_block: A comparison names both animals and states a precise difference in how they move.
bridge.passage: A fish travels with fins and a tail, but a frog kicks with paired legs. Both can move through pond water.
bridge.prompt: Write one sentence that contrasts how the fish and frog move in water.

concept_slots.description: States that the fish uses fins or its tail.
any_of: fish moves with fins and tail

concept_slots.description: States that the frog uses or kicks its legs.
any_of: frog moves through water with its legs

masterclass.teaching_block: Compare closely related animals with precise features instead of saying only that they look different.
masterclass.passage: The pond frog has smooth, moist-looking skin and often makes long jumps. The garden toad has bumpier, drier-looking skin and usually takes shorter hops.
masterclass.prompt: Write one sentence comparing both skin texture and movement.

concept_slots.description: Contrasts the frog's smoother skin with the toad's bumpier skin.
any_of: frog has smoother skin than the toad
frog has smooth skin while the toad is bumpy
toad has bumpier skin than the frog
frog is smoother but the toad is bumpier
frog's skin is smoother and the toad's is bumpier

concept_slots.description: Contrasts the frog's longer jumps with the toad's shorter hops.
any_of: frog jumps farther than the toad
and jumps farther than the toad
frog makes longer jumps than the toad
and makes longer jumps than the toad
toad takes shorter hops than the frog
frog makes long jumps while the toad takes shorter hops
frog jumps longer but the toad hops shorter

independent_check.teaching_block: Write an original comparison. Name both animals, include one similarity and one accurate difference, and connect the ideas clearly.
independent_check.passage: Field chart: a frog swims by kicking webbed back feet and can travel over wet ground; a silver fish swims with fins and remains in water; a toad is an amphibian that uses short hops and has less webbing between its toes.
independent_check.prompt: In 25 to 50 words, compare a frog with either the fish or the toad. Name both animals, give one accurate similarity, and give one accurate difference.

rubric_criteria.description: Contains 25 to 50 words.
Names the frog.
Names exactly one comparison animal: the fish or the toad.
States one accurate similarity for the selected pair: frog and fish both swim, or frog and toad are both amphibians or both move on land.
States one accurate difference for the selected pair involving habitat, fins and legs, skin, webbing, or hopping distance.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Compare a frog with a new water visitor by stating one shared ability and one precise body-feature difference.
transfer_check.passage: A frog paddles with long webbed back feet and can hop onto the bank. A duck paddles with two webbed feet but has feathers, wings, and a bill.
transfer_check.prompt: Write one clear comparison of the frog and duck that includes one similarity and one difference.

concept_slots.description: States that both animals swim or paddle with webbed feet.
any_of: frog and duck can both swim
each uses webbed feet in water

concept_slots.description: States an accurate difference in body covering or body parts.
any_of: duck has feathers but the frog does not
duck has wings and a bill
frog hops while the duck has wings
duck is feathered while the frog has smooth skin

levels.title: Connect the frog's calls
levels.focus: explain croaking with and, or, but, and because
levels.teaching_goal: Choose connectors that show addition, choice, contrast, or reason in complete sentences about frog calls.

guided_check.teaching_block: Use because to connect a result to its cause. When a male frog calls, air makes the inflated throat pouch vibrate and amplify the sound.
guided_check.passage: Air passes through the male frog's throat while its inflated pouch vibrates. This makes the call louder.
guided_check.prompt: Which sentence joins the ideas with a reason?
options: the call grows louder because the inflated throat pouch vibrates
the call grows louder but the inflated throat pouch vibrates
the call grows louder or the inflated throat pouch vibrates
the throat pouch vibrates because the call grows louder
accepted_answers: the call grows louder because the inflated throat pouch vibrates
the frog makes a louder call because its throat pouch vibrates
its call is amplified because the inflated pouch vibrates

bridge.teaching_block: Use but when two facts contrast. Repair the incomplete sentence by writing both ideas around the connector.
bridge.passage: The pond looks quiet in daylight. After sunset, many frog calls rise from the reeds.
bridge.prompt: Join the two facts in one complete sentence using but.
accepted_answers: the pond looks quiet in daylight, but many frog calls rise from the reeds after sunset
the pond is quiet during the day, but frogs call from the reeds after sunset
the pond seems quiet by day but fills with frog calls after sunset

masterclass.teaching_block: Use or to show alternatives and and to add a related fact. A stronger sentence can manage both relationships without confusing choice with addition.
masterclass.passage: A frog may call from the reeds. It may call from the muddy bank. In either place, its repeated croaks travel across the pond.
masterclass.prompt: Combine all three ideas in one complete sentence using or for the two calling places and and for the added fact.
accepted_answers: a frog may call from the reeds or the muddy bank, and its repeated croaks travel across the pond
the frog can call from the reeds or from the muddy bank and its repeated croaks carry across the pond
a frog calls either from the reeds or the muddy bank, and the repeated sound travels across the pond

independent_check.teaching_block: A fresh set of notes may contain more than one relationship. Decide how each pair of facts connects, then express both relationships clearly.
independent_check.passage: At dusk, a frog can call beside the drain. It can call from the grass. The grass is far from the pond. Its call still reaches the water.
independent_check.prompt: Write two complete connected ideas: one about the possible calling places and one about the distant call reaching the pond.

concept_slots.description: Uses a choice connector to link the drain and grass as alternative calling places.
any_of: either by the drain or among the grass
either beside the drain or from the grass

concept_slots.description: Uses a contrast relationship while stating that the grass is distant from the pond.
any_of: even though the grass is far
even though the grass is a long way
although the grass is a long way
grass is far from the pond but
grass is a long way from the pond but
despite the distance from the pond

concept_slots.description: States that the frog's call, voice, croak, or sound reaches the water or pond.

forbidden_phrases: calls from both places at the same time
the distant call cannot reach the pond
voice does not carry to the pond
the grass is beside the pond

transfer_check.teaching_block: Choose connectors by meaning in a fresh setting: because gives a reason, while but marks a contrast.
transfer_check.passage: The myna moved under the awning when rain began. The lane was noisy, yet its whistle remained easy to hear.
transfer_check.prompt: Write two complete sentences: use because to explain the move under the awning and but to contrast the noisy lane with the clear whistle.

concept_slots.description: Uses because to connect the rain with moving under the awning.
any_of: moved under the awning because it rained
went under the awning because rain began
because it was raining, the myna moved
because rain began the myna sheltered

concept_slots.description: Uses but to contrast the noisy lane with the audible whistle.
any_of: lane was noisy but its whistle was clear
it was noisy but the whistle could be heard
road was noisy but the myna was easy to hear
lane had noise but its whistle carried

forbidden_phrases: moved because the awning was dry

levels.title: Build a clear frog sentence
levels.focus: arrange jumbled words into grammatical sentences
levels.teaching_goal: Arrange a subject, action, and detail into a complete grammatical sentence.

guided_check.teaching_block: In a basic English sentence, place the subject before its action and put the action's detail after the verb.
guided_check.passage: Jumbled words: insect / an / catches / frog / the
guided_check.prompt: Which arrangement is a complete grammatical sentence?
options: The frog catches an insect.
The frog an insect catches.
The catches frog an insect.
The frog catches insect an.
accepted_answers: The frog catches an insect.
the frog catches an insect

bridge.teaching_block: Place an adverb where it clearly modifies the action. Quickly can come before swims or directly after it in this sentence.
bridge.passage: Near-correct line: The frog across the pond swims quickly.
bridge.prompt: Rewrite the line as a natural sentence. Place quickly before or after swims.
accepted_answers: the frog quickly swims across the pond
The frog quickly swims across the pond.
the frog swims quickly across the pond
The frog swims quickly across the pond.

masterclass.teaching_block: When one clause gives a reason, place because between the result clause and the cause clause, or begin with the cause clause and use a comma.
masterclass.passage: Jumbled clauses: the frog slips under a leaf / the sun is hot / because
masterclass.prompt: Order all three parts into one complete reason sentence.
accepted_answers: the frog slips under a leaf because the sun is hot
The frog slips under a leaf because the sun is hot.
because the sun is hot, the frog slips under a leaf
Because the sun is hot, the frog slips under a leaf.

independent_check.teaching_block: Reconstruct an unseen two-clause sentence by choosing the connective that matches the relationship. One connective does not belong.
independent_check.passage: Jumbled parts: the frog enters the pond / the bank is dry / because / and
independent_check.prompt: Arrange both clauses into one complete sentence that explains why the frog enters the pond, and leave out the extra connective.
accepted_answers: the frog enters the pond because the bank is dry
The frog enters the pond because the bank is dry.
because the bank is dry, the frog enters the pond
Because the bank is dry, the frog enters the pond.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Rebuild an unfamiliar sentence by placing the subject before its action and using because to introduce the cause.
transfer_check.passage: Jumbled parts: the children carry umbrellas / dark clouds gather / because / quickly
transfer_check.prompt: Arrange all the parts into one complete sentence. Place quickly where it naturally describes carry.
accepted_answers: the children quickly carry umbrellas because dark clouds gather
The children quickly carry umbrellas because dark clouds gather.
the children carry umbrellas quickly because dark clouds gather
The children carry umbrellas quickly because dark clouds gather.
because dark clouds gather, the children quickly carry umbrellas
Because dark clouds gather, the children quickly carry umbrellas.

levels.title: Reply to a pond-side friend
levels.focus: write a short friendly reply message
levels.teaching_goal: Write a relevant, friendly reply with a greeting, connected details, a question, and a closing.

guided_check.teaching_block: A friendly reply responds to what the sender said instead of starting an unrelated topic.
guided_check.passage: Hi Tara, I saw three tadpoles near the pond steps this morning. Have you noticed any changes in your pond? - Kabir
guided_check.prompt: Which opening responds directly to Kabir?
options: Hi Kabir, I saw tiny legs on our tadpoles yesterday.
Hi Kabir, ponds can contain many small animals.
Hi Tara, I saw tiny legs on our tadpoles yesterday.
Hi Kabir, did you finish the tadpole homework?
accepted_answers: Hi Kabir, I saw tiny legs on our tadpoles yesterday.
hi kabir i saw tiny legs on our tadpoles yesterday

bridge.teaching_block: Repair an incomplete reply by keeping its greeting, adding a relevant detail, and asking the sender a related question.
bridge.passage: Incomplete reply to Nisha's note about rainy-night croaks: Hi Nisha, I heard frogs too.
bridge.prompt: Rewrite the incomplete reply with the greeting, one detail about where or when you heard frogs, and one question for Nisha.

concept_slots.description: Includes a greeting to Nisha.
Adds where or when the writer heard frogs.
Asks Nisha a question about the frogs or calls.

forbidden_phrases: I did not read your note

masterclass.teaching_block: Before writing a full message, compose a greeting and two connected reply sentences: one answers the sender and one continues the exchange.
masterclass.passage: Dev asks whether you saw frogs at the park pond and what they were doing.
masterclass.prompt: Write a greeting to Dev, one sentence answering his question with a frog action, and one sentence asking Dev a related question.

concept_slots.description: Includes a greeting to Dev.
Answers whether the writer saw frogs.
any_of: I saw frogs at the park
I noticed frogs at the pond

concept_slots.description: Names an action by the observed frogs.
Asks Dev a related question.
any_of: how many frogs did you see

independent_check.teaching_block: Reply in your own words. Answer the sender, share two relevant details, ask one friendly question, and include a greeting and closing.
independent_check.passage: Hi! Our class visited a wetland today. I liked watching a frog vanish among green plants, and I wondered whether frogs visit your neighbourhood after rain. Write back soon! - Maya
independent_check.prompt: Write Maya a 35 to 60 word reply. Include a greeting to Maya, answer whether frogs visit after rain, share two relevant details, ask one related question, and end with a closing and your name.

rubric_criteria.description: Contains 35 to 60 words.
Includes a greeting addressed to Maya.
Answers whether frogs visit the writer's neighbourhood after rain.
Provides one relevant detail about frogs seen or heard after rain.
Provides a second distinct detail about frogs seen or heard after rain.
Asks Maya one question related to frogs, rain, or her wetland visit.
Ends with a friendly closing.
Includes the writer's name after the closing.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Use the friendly-message structure in a new exchange. Respond to the sender's news, add a relevant detail, ask a question, and close politely.
transfer_check.passage: Hello! I found a tiny frog beside our school rain garden after the storm. It stayed still until the puddle became quiet. Have you seen any small animals near your school? - Arjun
transfer_check.prompt: Write Arjun a 30 to 55 word reply with a greeting, a direct answer, one relevant observation, one related question, and a closing with your name.

rubric_criteria.description: Contains 30 to 55 words.
Greets Arjun and directly answers whether the writer has seen a small animal near school.
Adds one relevant observation about the animal, weather, or habitat.
Asks Arjun one related question about the frog or rain garden.
Ends with a friendly closing and the writer's name.

items.passage: A frog rests under a fern on a muddy bank, then dives into a stream when footsteps approach.
items.prompt: Which statement matches the whole observation?

concept_slots.description: Identifies the frog's use of the bank or fern shelter.
Identifies the frog's movement into the stream or water.
any_of: moves from the bank into the stream
enters the water when footsteps approach

items.passage: The ranger calls the tiny, newly hatched swimmer a larva. It has a tail and has not grown legs yet.
items.prompt: What does larva mean in this observation?

concept_slots.description: Identifies a larva as a young or newly hatched stage.
Connects the word to the tadpole or tailed larval stage before legs grow.

items.passage: Eggs float in a shaded pool. Small tadpoles hatch, grow legs, and gradually take the shape of adult frogs.
items.prompt: In one sentence, state the paragraph's main idea about the change from egg to adult frog.

concept_slots.description: States that eggs hatch into tadpoles.
States that tadpoles grow or change into adult frogs.

items.passage: The frog remains under a rock. The midday ground is hot and dry.
items.prompt: Join the facts as one complete sentence using because.

concept_slots.description: Uses because to connect the result and cause.
any_of: because the midday ground is hot
because the hot ground is dry

concept_slots.description: States that the frog remains or shelters under the rock.
States that the ground is hot or dry.

forbidden_phrases: leaves the rock because it is hot

items.passage: A moth hovers just beyond the frog's nose. The frog does not chase it; instead, its tongue darts out and returns.
items.prompt: Why is the tongue useful in this scene?
options: it reaches the moth quickly without a chase
it checks whether the moth is safe to eat
it knocks the moth onto the water for later
it guides the frog's jump towards the moth
accepted_answers: it reaches the moth quickly without a chase
the tongue lets the frog catch the moth quickly
it is useful because it catches prey without chasing it

items.passage: Word bank: webbed - joined by thin skin between the toes.
items.prompt: Use webbed correctly in a complete sentence about swimming.

concept_slots.description: Uses the word webbed to describe the frog's feet or toes.
Connects the webbed feet to swimming or pushing water.
any_of: webbed toes help the frog swim
uses its webbed feet to swim

items.passage: A tree frog chooses one calling place: a branch or a wall.
items.prompt: Which sentence correctly shows the choice between the two calling places?
options: A tree frog may call from a branch or from a wall.
A tree frog calls from a branch and a wall at the same time.
A tree frog calls from a branch because the wall is nearby.
A tree frog calls from a branch, but the wall is damp.
accepted_answers: A tree frog may call from a branch or from a wall.
a tree frog may call from a branch or from a wall

items.passage: Jumbled words: pond / the / across / swims / frog / the
items.prompt: Arrange every word into one complete grammatical sentence.
accepted_answers: the frog swims across the pond
The frog swims across the pond.

items.passage: A pale green frog settles against pale green duckweed. From above, its outline is difficult to separate from the plants.
items.prompt: What advantage does the matching colour provide?
options: predators may fail to notice the frog
the colour helps the frog choose matching plants
the pale pattern makes the frog look larger
the colour signals other frogs across the pond
accepted_answers: predators may fail to notice the frog
it helps hide the frog from predators
the matching colour makes the frog difficult to see

items.passage: At the start of the rainy season, several frogs call from separate puddles after dark.
items.prompt: Why might calling help frogs that are spread across the area? Answer in one sentence.

concept_slots.description: States that calling helps separated frogs hear, find, or communicate with one another.
any_of: calling helps them find each other
calls help them locate one another

items.passage: New comparison notes: a marsh frog crosses water with strong kicks and rests on wet soil; a stream fish steers with fins and stays below the water surface.
items.prompt: In 25 to 50 words, compare the frog and fish. Name both animals, give one accurate similarity, and give one accurate difference.

rubric_criteria.description: Contains 25 to 50 words.
Names the frog.
Names the fish.
States that both the frog and fish can swim or move through water.
States an accurate difference involving the fish's fins or water-only life and the frog's legs or use of land.

items.passage: On a cool morning, a frog warms itself on a flat brick beside a trough. At a sudden shout, it jumps into the trough.
items.prompt: Which detail shows the frog moving from land to water?
options: it jumps from the brick into the trough
the morning air feels cool
someone gives a sudden shout
the brick lies flat
accepted_answers: it jumps from the brick into the trough
the frog jumps into the trough
it leaves the brick and enters the water

items.passage: The guide says that a water snake is a predator of small frogs because it hunts and eats them.
items.prompt: What does predator mean in this sentence?
